The Chinese silver pomfret Pampus chinensis is a commercially important scombriform fish that inhabits coastal waters of the Indo-West Pacific region. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges from a small, transparent pelagic egg with a wet weight of only 0.0008 grams [Wwb = 0.0008 grams]. This minimal mass at birth reflects the modest egg diameter characteristic of the genus and underscores the extreme vulnerability of the early life stages. During the yolk-sac phase, the protolarva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves while rapidly developing its mouthparts and digestive tract. The exotrophic transition is a critical bottleneck: the small initial size means that first-feeding larvae must encounter appropriately sized zooplankton prey within a narrow window following yolk absorption, or they face starvation. Researchers have noted that the lecithotrophic period is brief, with the mouth opening and swim bladder inflation occurring within a few days after eclosion under optimal conditions. The larvae then progress through a series of transformations as they develop squamation and fin rays, gradually assuming the compressed, deep-bodied morphology that typifies adult pomfrets.

As the juveniles grow, they exhibit a pronounced shift in body proportions, attaining a total length at puberty of 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters] and a corresponding wet weight at puberty of approximately 143 grams [Wwp = approximately 143 grams]. These values indicate that sexual maturation occurs at about half the ultimate total length observed in the population. The body mass at puberty is derived from the species' length-weight relationship, which is strongly allometric and consistent with the deep body shape characteristic of the genus. The onset of gonadal maturation involves activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, with vitellogenesis beginning in females and spermiation initiating in males. In field-collected specimens, puberty is typically reached during the second year of life, though this can vary with local temperature regimes and food availability. The attainment of 20 centimeters total length marks a clear developmental milestone: before this point, energy is primarily channeled into somatic growth and the build-up of lipid reserves, whereas afterwards a growing proportion of resources is redirected toward reproductive tissues and gamete production.

Reproductive output in Pampus chinensis has been quantified through fecundity studies that take advantage of the well-established relationship between female size and egg number. Under typical thermal conditions of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], a female at the end of the spawning season is capable of producing approximately 221,894 eggs per season [Ri = approximately 221,894 eggs per season], with a single spawning event occurring each year [F_R_i = single spawning event occurring each year]. This annual reproductive effort is considerable for a fish of its size and reflects an iteroparous strategy in which adults may spawn repeatedly across several breeding seasons. The species is a batch spawner, releasing its pelagic eggs in multiple episodes over the course of the spawning period, which typically coincides with warmer months when planktonic food resources for the larvae are most abundant. Interestingly, the fecundity estimate used for Pampus chinensis was derived from data on the congener Pampus argenteus, after scaling by the cube of the length ratio, providing a robust proxy for the maximum reproductive output of this species.

The ultimate total length attained by the Chinese silver pomfret is approximately 40 centimeters [Li = approximately 40 centimeters], which corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of about 1154 grams [Wwi = about 1154 grams]. This asymptotic size is reached after several years of sustained growth, during which the fish accumulate substantial somatic tissue, particularly in the form of the deep, laterally compressed musculature that powers their sustained swimming. The length-weight relationship describing this species is W = 0.01738 * L to the power of 3.01, indicating near-isometric scaling of body mass with length. In the wild, maximum sizes are typically recorded from offshore trawl surveys, with individuals exceeding 40 centimeters being relatively rare. The ecological significance of attaining a large adult size includes reduced vulnerability to gape-limited predators, increased fecundity associated with larger body volume, and greater competitive ability during foraging. Comparisons with other stromateoid fishes reveal that Pampus chinensis occupies an intermediate position on the size spectrum, being considerably larger than the smaller genus Peprilus but smaller than some of the larger pomfret species found in the eastern Atlantic. The large body mass also provides a substantial buffer against seasonal fluctuations in prey availability.

Longevity in Pampus chinensis has been estimated from otolith annuli and length-frequency analysis, with the oldest documented individuals reaching 7 years [am = 7 years] of age under the ambient thermal conditions typical of its subtropical range, approximately 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This maximum lifespan is relatively modest among marine teleosts, which can often exceed several decades in cooler waters. The relatively short lifespan is consistent with the species' position as a moderately fast-growing, early-maturing fish that experiences fairly high natural mortality rates, particularly among juveniles. Age validation through marginal increment analysis confirms annual periodicity in otolith growth zones, providing confidence in the longevity estimate. The combination of early maturation at 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters] length and 143 grams [Wwp = 143 grams], coupled with a lifespan of 7 years, yields a life-history strategy that emphasizes moderate reproductive output spread across several years rather than a single massive spawning event. This schedule is well suited to the variable coastal environments the species inhabits, where interannual fluctuations in productivity can strongly affect recruitment success. The 7-year maximum also means that most individuals will experience only a handful of spawning seasons during their lifetime.
